correctness.rationale: For odd support \(p<q\), the abundancy ratio is strictly below \(p/(p-1)\,q/(q-1)\le15/8<2\). For \(n=2^a p^b\), setting \(B=2^{a+1}\) turns abundance into \((B-p)p^b>B-1\) and deficiency of \(n/p\) into \((B-p)p^{b-1}<B-1\). These inequalities exclude \(b\ge2\). For \(b=1\), abundance and deficiency of \(n/2\) give exactly \(2^a<p<2^{a+1}-1\). The resulting non-Mersenne-prime bijection gives the exact count. The prime number theorem is then applied only on \(U/y\in[1,2]\), where its usual asymptotic is uniform, and the Mersenne correction is \(O(\log X)\).
risks: The finite replay is not used to justify the infinite asymptotic; the asymptotic depends on the symbolic classification and the prime number theorem.

value.rationale: Exactly two distinct prime factors form the minimal nontrivial support on which strict primitive abundant numbers occur. The theorem gives a complete exact counting identity and reveals a nonconvergent normalized asymptotic with explicit phase and extremal constants, rather than merely extending a finite table. This is a natural quantitative boundary case for the classical global distribution problem and provides a benchmark showing that fixed-support counts can exhibit log-periodic oscillation even when the ambient counting problem has a very different scale.
risks: The proof after the classical classification is elementary and uses only the prime number theorem; its value is the exact phase description, not technical depth.
